doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Leonard Feather and arranging for the BBC in London
summary: Feather cabled him to write for the BBC radio staff band; he wrote about three arrangements a week and could not get a permit to play.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Eventually you went to England, and that, I believe came about through your friend, long-term friend, Leonard Feather.

That’s right. We had never met, and I got a cable from Leonard, asking me if I would be interested in coming to London [England] to work for the BBC [British Broadcasting Company] as an arranger. That was very interesting to me. I corresponded with him and answered, of course, in the affirmative, and he worked out a deal with the BBC for me to come there. I think I went there in March of maybe 1936.
The arrangements for the BBC were a somewhat different instrumentation than the so-called dance band or big band writing you had been doing. What sort of instrumentation was involved in your . . .

Oh, boy. It’s kind of silly of me to say this, but I don’t remember. A couple of trumpets, maybe three. I don’t remember what the brass section and saxophone section and the rhythm section . . . I know that . . . I don’t know. I don’t know, but it was, you know, what was the radio staff band at that time.
And it had a string section at this time.
Yeah, it had some strings, yes.
You were not playing with him. You were just writing.
No, I didn’t play at all.
I couldn’t get a permit to play in England at the time.
So you were basically a full-time writer for the band.
What sort of output did you have to [produce] for them for a weekly . . .
If I remember correctly, I think I did about three arrangements a week. [unclear] to something that I did on the Lucky Strike Hit Parade show later in 1941.

Do you remember y our own feelings about undertaking this, which was, after all, very different from what you had been doing? Was there any sense of trepidation or, you know, moving into a new country, a new type of orchestra, a string section and . . .

No. For some reason, I’ve never known fear and trepidation. [Berger laughs.] But, you know, I just went in and found out what they wanted and did what I was supposed to do. [I] liked living in London, and I still like visiting there. It’s one of my favorite cities on the globe.
